item.title: Comedian Alfred Robles wears many hats: Cowboy, Catholic and crowd therapist
item.description: Alfred Robles reveals why fans say he wears his signature tejana wrong, and how Gabriel "Fluffy" Iglesias pushed him from blurry photos to headliner.
item.content:encoded:
After Alfred Robles’ career took off, he started noticing something funny on the comedy circuit: other comics adopted cowboy hats of their own, hoping for a piece of the magic that turned him into a headliner.

"Everybody thought that I started blowing up because of the hat. After that, I saw a bunch of comedians wearing hats waiting to blow up," Robles told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview following the release of his new YouTube stand-up special, "El Cowboy."

The irony is that Robles’ signature tejana didn't start as a branding play at all, and according to the older guys in his community, he’s not even wearing it right.

"The crazy part is there's a wrong way to wear a hat, and I wear it the wrong way," the East L.A.-raised comic said, explaining that the hat is "supposed" to be worn low so it covers your eyes.

"I get a lot of older Mexicans [who] come up to me [saying], 'I love it, but you wear it wrong.' I go, 'I know, I get it, bro. But the reason why I do it is because I'm being filmed, and I want them to see my eyes and my face and all that.'"

"'You're still wearing it wrong!'" the cowboy hat purists say.

For Robles, the hat isn’t a calculated gimmick. It’s just a piece of his background adjusted to fit the stage, much like the rest of his unconventional path to headlining.

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

Before he was headlining theaters and dropping back-to-back comedy specials, the East L.A. native tried on plenty of other roles: police academy cadet, retail security guard, shaky-handed tour photographer and reluctant caretaker — all before becoming a tequila-pouring comedy therapist for hundreds of strangers a night, with a little help from renowned stand-up comedian Gabriel "Fluffy" Iglesias along the way.

Comedy wasn't part of the neighborhood curriculum growing up in East L.A. (and don't confuse it with neighboring Boyle Heights, a distinction Robles still guards with hometown pride). Nobody around Robles was talking about open mics, aside from his childhood friend Jay Hernandez, who the comedian said treated acting like an inevitable business plan long before landing his starring role in the "Magnum P.I." reboot and other Hollywood credits.

For Robles, stand-up only came into focus after his first career choice fell apart.

He first enrolled in the police academy before being disqualified due to a restraining order filed by an ex-girlfriend in his early 20s.

"It was a long time ago. I was innocent, guys."

"And then, right after I got kicked out from the police academy, I went straight into comedy," he said, recalling that he used to write jokes and poems in high school.

DAVID CROSS DOESN’T 'GIVE A F---’: THE ACTOR-COMEDIAN ON HIS NEW SPECIAL, SOCIAL MEDIA AND ‘TERRIFYING’ AI

"I said to myself, maybe that was my calling — is to become a comedian."

At the time, Robles was living with his mother and working a loss prevention job at Old Navy.

"In the early 2000s I was making $17 an hour. So that was a lot of money," he said. "So I went from $17 an hour, 40 hours a week, to getting paid drink tickets."

He said his mother was skeptical at first, but that he was glad she was still around to see his success, even if she doesn't understand enough English to really get his jokes.

"The only positive thing she said was, 'You know what? I didn't understand you, but the people were laughing, and I was proud,'" he said.

That was good enough for him.

His big break arrived a few years into his open-mic grind in the early 2000s at a bar show in Montebello, California, when Iglesias pulled him aside with a blunt piece of advice: cut the profanity.

"He goes, 'You cuss a lot. I know you don't need your cussing because you don't say it in your punchlines. You'll just clean that up, and you'll go far,'" Robles recalled.

He was resistant at first, but cleaned up his set anyway. Iglesias saw the difference and invited Robles on the road in 2010, though not as an opener.

"He told me, 'You know what, I'm going to give you a spot, but you're not going to go up on stage, you're going to take pictures for me,'" Robles said.

JEFF ARCURI REVEALS HOW 'BACHELORETTE' WIFE’S CANCER FIGHT TRANSFORMED HIS COMEDY — AND THEIR MARRIAGE

"I'm not even a photographer, bro. I don't even know a camera... The messed-up part is my hands shake, so every picture was messed up."

"Anything to get your foot in," Robles maintained. "That's the way I saw it."

Those blurry photos eventually turned into five-minute sets, then 10-minute spots, and eventually led to Robles performing at arenas like Madison Square Garden and Dodger Stadium alongside Iglesias. Still, Robles knew he couldn't build a legacy as someone else's opener.

"I didn't do comedy to become someone's friend. I said, 'You know, I got to start my own life. I got to start my career.' I don't want to go thinking, 'Oh, I never tried it, to go on my own.'"

He hired a videographer friend of his, with whom he has now been working for nearly four years.

"We grew together. And now I'm here headlining across the country. And it was because I took a risk on myself, and I bet on myself. And I started posting clips up, and the clips blew up."

The momentum snowballed into a massive recent run, capped by releasing two specials within two months of each other. The first was a Kevin Hart-produced half-hour on Hulu in September, and the second was his new hour, "El Cowboy," which dropped in November.

Robles' comedy routine begins with around 45–50 minutes of traditional stand-up before he starts to "mess around" and bring people up on stage.

It all started because he likes crowd work, and he used to enjoy playing matchmaker by bringing single people in his audience on stage. Then, one onlooker raised his hand and, instead of looking for a hook-up, wanted an outlet to share a problem.

"So he came up onstage, and he just told me a sad story. And I go, 'Bro, do you want a shot?'"

He did.

COMEDIAN MATT RIFE SAYS HE DITCHED HOLLYWOOD'S OLD PLAYBOOK FOR SUCCESS AFTER HITTING 'ROCK BOTTOM'

"So I give him a shot and just, that took me to another level ... So now, at the end of the show, I just ask them, 'Hey, whoever's going through a problem or just has a story they want to share with me, we'll take a shot together.'"

Robles speculated that speaking openly about his own experiences set the stage for everybody else to open up.

"And then the alcohol helps. Now we're all crying, bro," he laughed.

The unfiltered nature of the audience-interaction portion of Robles' show occasionally leads to unexpected places, Robles told Fox News Digital. One woman's story about sleeping with an ex during a two-day breakup with her baby's father and what followed prompted Robles to blur her face in his clips, even though she never asked him to.

But it has also led him to shoot eight episodes of a series "kind of like 'The Jerry Springer Show'" focused on the audience participation piece of his act that he now wants to pitch.

"My stuff is just all real, bro. They're real problems, real people, man. So people love that. People love problems, as long as it's not your problem."

The candor of the crowd is cultivated by Robles' own honest discussion of topics that could be considered taboo in Mexican-American culture, like men's health and aging.

"El Cowboy" features a bit about Robles' first time having enough money to afford a visit to the doctor's office and the unexpected prostate exam that followed.

"The reason why I say it a lot, too — and I love that joke — is because, in my culture, Mexican men don't want to go have your prostate checked," Robles said, adding that nowadays you can get a blood test instead of a digital rectal exam.

"They still don't even want to do that because a lot of them don't want to know. For whatever reason, that's big in our culture. They do not want to know, and I'm over here trying to tell them, 'Hey bro, you got to know, man! You could save your life,'" he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"We just feel like, if we know, and we tell someone else, now we put, like, a burden on them. Now they're going to feel sorry for us, and I don't want that to happen. And that's something I want to break."

One friend of his lost a toe to diabetes, to which Robles said, "If you would have went to the doctor, bro, a year before, you would've had a toe."

Another friend had a stroke while working at Disneyland, and instead of seeking help for his symptoms, he left the park to have the stroke in his car because he didn't want to bother anyone.

"Well, you could have died, fool," Robles said. "You would have died in the happiest place in the world."

Beneath the on-stage bravado, the cowboy hat and the late-night tequila shots sits one more role that anchors everything else: a grounded Catholic kid from East L.A. who still relies on quiet faith.

Robles admitted he hasn't been to church in a while, but prayer remains a constant rhythm in his day.

"I pray when I wake up, and I pray at night ... I mean I forget here and there, but I always catch myself praying. You know, when I jump on a flight, when I jump on the freeway ... When I'm sitting down just having my own thoughts, that's when I pray," he said.

"I never lost faith, bro. I just grinded and grinded and prayed and prayed, and here I am."

Even with a new special in the works and an unscripted TV project ready to pitch, Robles doesn't measure his career by what’s still on the horizon. After years of wearing many hats, he’s content with where things stand.

"My dream? I'm already living my dream, man. Whatever happens, happens, bro. I'm cool if it does, and I'm cool if it doesn't," he said.

"Like I said earlier, bro, I didn't do this to be someone's friend. I didn't do this to blow up. I did it because I love comedy. The rest is just extra, bro, and I am cool with that."

item.title: DANNY DANON: From Auschwitz to the UN, Israel must never retreat
item.description: Dozens of United Nations ambassadors walked through Auschwitz as antisemitism surges, and Israel's envoy says the next secretary-general must act.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this month, at a time when antisemitism is surging around the world, I walked with dozens of United Nations ambassadors through the haunted gates of Auschwitz.

No matter how many times I return to that hallowed ground, the experience never becomes easier. Each visit reminds me of the devastating cost of antisemitism and the catastrophic consequences of a world that remains silent in the face of hatred.

This diplomatic mission came at a critical moment. The race to elect the next U.N. secretary-general is advancing quickly. Whoever assumes this position must confront the institutional antisemitism that has taken root within the U.N.

AMBASSADOR JEFF BARTOS: UN MUST ABANDON ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-WESTERN LEGACY OF DURBAN CONFERENCE

This institutional antisemitism is prevalent throughout the U.N. Headquarters. We hear it from U.N. officials, read it in U.N. reports and even encounter it in the secretary-general’s own rhetoric. An institution founded in the aftermath of the Holocaust can't claim to fight antisemitism while providing a platform for the demonization of Israel.

As representatives of the Jewish state, we have a responsibility to address this issue. But we cannot do it alone. We must leverage our diplomatic relationships to build coalitions with other nations and ensure that combating antisemitism becomes a collective international priority.

That is why, in September, we established a task force of U.N. member states to combat antisemitism within the organization and around the world. At our inaugural meeting, we focused on translating declarations against Jew hatred into concrete action. The next secretary-general must build on these efforts, not allow them to fade into another round of empty promises.

Our mission to Poland was a natural extension of that work. We must ensure that the memory of the Holocaust remains permanently etched in the international community’s consciousness. Never again means nothing if the world forgets what happened before.

THE ANTISEMITISM HORSESHOE IS PLAYING OUT IN REAL TIME — FROM NEW YORK TO PARIS AND BEYOND

For many of the ambassadors accompanying me, this was their first encounter with the remnants of the Holocaust. They had studied it, heard about it and read about it. But nothing compares to standing on the very ground where the Nazis committed their atrocities.

Witnessing history is only the beginning. My colleagues must return to their countries determined to confront antisemitism not just at the U.N., but in their own countries as well.

Around the world, 2025 was the deadliest year for antisemitic violence in three decades, with more than twenty people killed in at least four attacks.

In the United States, FBI data shows that antisemitism remains the most prevalent form of religiously motivated hate crime. Although Jews account for less than 3% of the population, they were targeted in 63% of religiously motivated hate crimes in 2025.

And this wave of hatred has not yet broken. Earlier this month, on the eve of Kristallnacht, an anti-Israel bike rally targeted Jewish and Israeli-owned restaurants in Philadelphia, accusing them of supporting "genocide." The rhetoric echoed familiar antisemitic patterns of prewar Europe: demonize Jews, assign collective guilt and turn hatred into a campaign of intimidation.

Being in Poland allowed me to confront these realities alongside my colleagues against the backdrop of history. But the most important part of this mission came when I brought the delegation to Israel.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

There, I showed my colleagues the beauty of our country, the strength of our people and the challenges we continue to face. They visited the sites of the Oct. 7 massacre and received informative briefings on the realities Israel confronts.

The visit underscored why a strong, independent Jewish state is indispensable. Israel is not merely a refuge from antisemitism. It is the eternal homeland of the Jewish people; a country capable of defending its people, preserving its history and shaping its own future.

At a time when many question whether Israel should continue engaging with the U.N., this mission reinforces exactly why we must.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Despite the relentless hostility Israel faces within the organization, we cannot afford to abandon the battlefield. We must remain, confront the lies, challenge the bias and find creative ways to achieve meaningful diplomatic victories.

Fighting antisemitism requires education, firsthand encounters with history and conversations that challenge entrenched misconceptions about Israel and the Jewish people.

Most importantly, fighting antisemitism requires leadership. The next secretary-general will inherit an institution facing a profound credibility crisis. Combating antisemitism must be more than another campaign promise. It must become a defining test of leadership for every candidate.

The diplomats who joined this mission learned a powerful lesson that no meeting or lecture could convey: we must confront hatred before it becomes catastrophe. Speeches alone are not sufficient to combat antisemitism. It requires concrete action, institutional accountability and a willingness to confront those who spread hatred.

We will take that lesson back to the United Nations. We will continue building coalitions, challenging antisemitism and demanding that the institution live up to the principles on which it was founded.

The next secretary-general will have a choice: confront antisemitism or allow it to continue poisoning the United Nations. We intend to make sure that choice cannot be ignored.

item.title: 400-year-old shipwreck lock finally opened after researchers crack secret code: 'Incredibly satisfying'
item.description: Revealing the code ANCE, a 400-year-old combination lock from the Ann Francis shipwreck was cracked by scientists using micro-CT scanning at Cardiff University.
item.content:encoded:
A 400-year-old brass lock recovered from a 16th-century shipwreck off the coast of Wales has finally been opened — and researchers didn't need a key to crack it.

The discovery, conducted as a joint effort between Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) and Cardiff University, was announced earlier this month. 

Museum officials said in a statement that the brass lock had "remained firmly locked" since its vessel was destroyed off the coast of Wales in the 16th century.

DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS

The Ann Francis was overtaken by a storm on Dec. 28, 1583, while returning from Spain. 

It was blown off course before wrecking on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot.

More than 400 years later, metal detectorist Peter Hughes began unearthing parts of the ship's hoard on Margam Beach in 1996.

He continued recovering artifacts from the site through 2017 — including the brass lock — after dredging and storms stripped away layers of sand.

Speaking to officials, Hughes said he was "immediately astonished" when he uncovered the lock.

TREASURE HUNTER STRIKES GOLD WITH 1,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY LINKED TO 'HAND OF GOD'

"When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief," he said, as Cardiff University reported.

"I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things [in] the treasure chest it once locked."

Researchers revealed the four-letter combination that kept it sealed for more than four centuries: ANCE.

To crack the code without damaging the artifact, museum experts partnered with specialists at Cardiff University to examine the lock's internal mechanism using CT scanning technology.

'SPECTACULAR' SHIPWRECK FOUND WITH UNDERWATER TIME CAPSULE OF UNTOUCHED CARGO: 'AMAZING FIND'

David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said micro-CT scanning allowed him to inspect the interior of the lock without harming it.

"By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination," said Williams, according to Cardiff University.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," he said.

After waiting until later that evening for museum officials to test the code, Williams got the news that it worked.

"Getting the message that we'd cracked it was incredibly satisfying," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Alastair Willis, a senior curator at Amgueddfa Cymru, said the meaning behind the lock's code remains unknown.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve," said Willis, the release noted.

He added, "Of course, now [that] we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

Officials said the lock is believed to have once secured a small chest holding valuables.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Because it was found near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights, researchers think it may have protected those items or a chest containing organic materials that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.

The hoard also included rare gold coins dating to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, as well as a boatswain's whistle.

The combination lock and other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard are now on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Recent archaeological and historical finds across Wales have drawn similar attention.

Earlier this year, archaeologists revealed new findings from a remote Roman fort in Wales — including fourth-century coins and artifacts — that may link the site to a centuries-old legend about Emperor Magnus Maximus.

Last winter, volunteers cleaning a South Wales beach uncovered roughly 200 mysterious old-fashioned shoes that may have washed ashore from a 19th-century shipwreck.

item.title: Virginia school district defends Thanksgiving 'Day of Mourning' resources for kids as young as third grade
item.description: Loudoun County Public Schools defends Thanksgiving resources describing the holiday as a "Day of Mourning" for some Native Americans, per watchdog report.
item.content:encoded:
A Virginia school district at the center of past education controversies is defending Thanksgiving "resources" for children as young as third grade that describes the holiday as a "Day of Mourning" for some Native Americans, according to documents obtained by the watchdog group Protect the Public's Trust.

"The Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS) Resources for Recognition Days & Months guide does not label Thanksgiving a ‘Day of Mourning,’" LCPS Communications told Fox News Digital in a statement Wednesday. "Rather, it includes multiple suggested resources that explore Thanksgiving traditions and historical perspectives, including Native American perspectives."

Loudoun County Public Schools, located outside Washington, D.C., includes the "resources" in a district resource guide for teachers, according to a Washington Free Beacon report. The materials also reportedly featured a Columbus Day lesson described as a "Debated Celebration," while Christmas does not appear in the guide's listed holiday resources.

LOUDOUN SCHOOL BOARD URGES STUDENTS TO ‘CELEBRATE’ LGBTQ+ HISTORY IN NEW PROCLAMATION

A slide for grades 3–5 labeled "The Real Story of Thanksgiving," shared by The Washington Free Beacon, reads, "Some Native American groups protest Thanksgiving as a Day of Mourning. They claim that the arrival of European explorers and settlers is not a cause for celebration, because it began the ill-treatment and deaths of millions of Native Americans. For them, Thanksgiving marks the beginning of a long period of violence and discrimination."

LCPS Communications went on to say that the guide contains optional teaching materials rather than mandatory curriculum, noting that educators are not required to use any specific lessons or activities. The district said the resources include materials from the Virginia Department of Education as well as supplementary content, and that teachers are encouraged to determine which materials are appropriate for their individual classrooms.

VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT FACES PROBE OVER 9/11 TEACHING GUIDE TELLING TEACHERS NOT TO ‘CENTER THE EXTREMISTS’

"Thanksgiving is included in the LCPS curriculum and is taught in accordance with Virginia’s History and Social Science Standards of Learning," LCPS Communications continued. "In second grade, students learn about Thanksgiving traditions and the origins of the holiday. Instruction also includes opportunities to learn about Native American history and perspectives, including the Wampanoag tribe."

LCPS added that it is "intentional about ensuring students have opportunities to learn history through multiple perspectives and develop a more complete understanding of historical events. Instruction is designed to be age-appropriate and aligned with students’ developmental levels."

HOW VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SHAMES KIDS TO MARK THANKSGIVING

The Washington Free Beacon also reported that a district-approved Thanksgiving lesson for middle and high school students, titled "Thanksgiving: A Day of Mixed Blessings," features a HuffPost-produced video examining why some Native Americans observe a National Day of Mourning on Thanksgiving. The video opens with a man invoking Malcolm X's famous remarks about Plymouth Rock to describe the arrival of European settlers from a Native American perspective.

Loudoun County Public Schools said its resource guide includes materials addressing both Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day, consistent with Virginia’s educational standards. The district added that the guide does not include dedicated resources for religious holidays such as Christmas, Hanukkah, Eid and Diwali, but said those holidays are covered in the elementary curriculum under state standards.

"LCPS remains committed to providing a high-quality education that meets the needs of all students and prepares them for future success," LCPS Communications added.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Alexa Moutevelis, Protect the Public's Trust communications director, said, "From introducing elementary school students to LGBTQ pride to teaching children that Thanksgiving is a ‘Day of Mourning,’ Loudoun County seems determined to filter American history and traditions through a DEI lens. There’s nothing wrong with teaching the complicated parts of American history, but these materials seem to emphasize grievance, oppression, and critical interpretations."

Moutevelis added, "It’s a good reminder for parents to pay attention to messages their children are receiving in the classroom and how public schools are choosing to frame important holidays and historical events."

item.title: Slain student’s family faces first Thanksgiving without her, blames missed chances to stop illegal alien
item.description: Sheridan Gorman's parents share their first Thanksgiving without their daughter, saying Chicago authorities missed chances to arrest the suspect.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The parents of an 18-year-old college student allegedly killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago are preparing for their first Thanksgiving without their daughter, as they grapple with an empty seat at the table and what they believe to be missed opportunities to prevent her death.

In an emotional Zoom interview with Fox News Digital, Sheridan Gorman's parents, Thomas and Jessica Gorman, remembered their daughter's love for the holidays while saying they're frustrated over what they believe were several missed opportunities by Chicago authorities to arrest the illegal immigrant accused of killing her.

Jose Medina-Medina, 25, was arrested after he allegedly killed Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student, on March 19. According to the Department of Homeland Security, he illegally entered the U.S. from Venezuela in 2023, when he was apprehended but released into the country by the Biden administration. He has pleaded not guilty to murder, attempted murder, aggravated assault, aggravated discharge of a firearm, and illegal possession of a weapon.

ANGEL FAMILIES PLEAD WITH LEADERS TO 'CHOOSE' AMERICAN CHILDREN OVER PROTECTING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

The Gormans said Sheridan's favorite Thanksgiving tradition was making apple pie. This year, her parents will continue that tradition without her, and said they plan to leave an empty seat at the dinner table.

"We're going to share an apple pie together and try to start, I guess, some new memories," Sheridan's father said. "As hard as it is without her, it's definitely going to be an empty seat at the table."

Sheridan's mother said the family usually gathers around the Thanksgiving table to share what they're thankful for, but this year will be different.

"I guess this year for us, it's going to be gratitude and grief at the same time," she said. "I think we're thankful that we had 18 years with her. The grief part is I wish we had so many more."

SHERIDAN GORMAN'S PARENTS SAY PROTECTING CHILDREN FROM FAILED IMMIGRATION POLICIES ISN'T A ONE-PARTY FIGHT

More than seven months after Gorman's death, her dogs still sit by her bedroom window, waiting for her to come home.

"Our dogs actually still sit in her bedroom window every day waiting for her to come home. It's been over seven months and that's where they are all day, just waiting," Jessica Gorman said.

BIDEN BORDER OFFICIALS RELEASED ALLEGED KILLER OF CHICAGO STUDENT 'DUE TO LACK OF SPACE,' DOCUMENTS SHOW

Prosecutors said during an earlier detention hearing for Medina-Medina on April 3 that Gorman was with her friends at a Rogers Park pier when she looked around a lighthouse and saw Medina-Medina was there. Gorman then walked back toward her friends and mouthed, "There's a man behind the lighthouse," at which point Medina-Medina began chasing them.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Court documents earlier obtained by Fox News Digital show that Medina-Medina told officials he was living at Leone Beach Park fieldhouse in Rogers Park in 2023, which was being used as a city-sponsored shelter for migrants.

WATCH: ANGEL MOM TURNS TABLES ON SANCTUARY POLITICIANS WITH BASIC QUESTION ABOUT THEIR PRIORITIES

Medina-Medina was arrested in 2023 and charged with shoplifting after he allegedly stole just over $130 in merchandise from a Macy's in downtown Chicago. He failed to appear for court hearings related to that case, and an arrest warrant remained active until the alleged murder.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Medina-Medina's attorney also said he suffers from epilepsy and still has bullet fragments lodged in his brain. The murder suspect turned himself in at the Texas border in 2023, where he was held in detention before being released. His attorney said that Medina-Medina had requested to be sent back to Colombia, where his mother had moved, but he was transported by bus to Chicago.

FATHER OF SLAIN STUDENT SHERIDAN GORMAN CALLS DEATH A 'FAILURE' AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S NOT GUILTY PLEA

Despite failing to appear for court hearings and living in city-funded housing, Medina-Medina wasn't arrested until after he was accused of fatally shooting Gorman. Thomas Gorman said "multiple" opportunities were missed to stop the murder suspect.

SEND US A TIP

"We made one mistake. We made a mistake sending our daughter to a school in Chicago. Sending our daughter to a sanctuary city. We had no idea," Jessica Gorman said.

WATCH: Slain college student's parents blast missed chances to stop illegal immigrant accused of murder

The Gormans said neither Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson nor Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker called them after Sheridan died. They have one pointed question for both officials:

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"What if Sheridan were your daughter? Again, would these policies, would these decisions, would these ridiculous explanations you give be enough for you?" they asked.

Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson and Pritzker for comment.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Just two days before she died, Gorman found out she was accepted into an internship program at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. Her mother said the college student was "really thrilled to spend that time in cowboy boots with her sister," which she never got to do.

As Gorman's family prepares for their first Thanksgiving without her, her mother said she'll miss the simple moments with her daughter the most.

item.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: Why angels remind us to give thanks and never lose hope on Thanksgiving
item.description: The Hebrew Bible's visions of angels and thanksgiving echo in survivor Chris Smith's near-death experience, a two-month coma, and a message of gratitude.
item.content:encoded:
In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Isaiah describes God sitting on an exalted throne, with seraphim angels attending to him and proclaiming his glory. This is an act of Thanksgiving (Isaiah 6:1–3). In the New Testament, specifically in the Book of Revelation, there are several scenes of heavenly worship and Thanksgiving, with living creatures falling down before God’s throne and giving thanks, worshiping his glory, honor and power over all things. They offer a collective Thanksgiving (Revelation 4:8–11; Revelation 7:11–12).

In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," there are many stories of survivors who have received messengers from God and survived near-death experiences, giving back to the Lord by doing good deeds for others. This is in the spirit of Thanksgiving. Spiritual leader Basye Holland-Shuey survives three cancers thanks to the intervention of angels, and becomes a spiritual leader and teacher. Suicidal alcoholic Bill Wilson sees God’s angels in a bright light on a mountaintop and gives thanks for this lifesaving vision by forming Alcoholics Anonymous, sharing his suffering and gratitude to God to help cure alcoholics everywhere.

DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US'--A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED

On Thanksgiving Eve in 2021, as described in "The Angels Among Us," Chris Smith goes on a first date with Leslie Reeves. They return to his place and warm a pizza in the oven, but Reeves’s former boyfriend, who has been stalking her, breaks in through the back door and shoots them both in the head. She is killed, but he manages to survive thanks to a visitation from heaven by his father, who died when Chris was 8 years old.

Chris remains on the floor bleeding as his dog scratches his chest and tries to revive him. He experiences being in a dark room, sitting at a long wooden table. He can see light over to his left side. It is an otherworldly, heavenly light. There are three beings there with him: Roy, Dave and John. John says, "Chris, we are three angels here to care for you. We are here to save you."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Chris says that after that, he is in a doorway where everything is lush and green. His father appears and says he is here to get Chris to a hospital. The next thing Chris knows, he is floating down the road in a vehicle, riding in the air above the pavement.

In the waking world, when Chris doesn’t show up for Thanksgiving dinner, a young girl named Brijon is sent over to his house, where she finds blood everywhere and calls 911.

But in the world inside Chris’s coma, his father proves his existence by telling Chris that his best friend Brad put two marijuana joints in his coat pocket while he was in the casket. Only Brad and Chris’s mother know about this, and when Chris wakes up from his coma two months later, his mother, Sharon, breaks into tears, verifying the story, as does Brad. Sharon relays this to me in an interview. Chris’s doctors are amazed that with a bullet in the right frontal lobe of his brain, his thoughts and speech are still clear. And then, with the help of much rehab and mesenchymal stem cell treatments, he goes on to regain the strength and function on the left side of his body.

In a great message for Thanksgiving, he dedicates his life to "helping young people understand the dangers of internet dating and domestic violence, and restoring faith in God to as many as I can around the world."

item.description: No. 2 Utah leads a Big 12 surge while Miami and Wake Forest chase ACC glory, as the latest CFP rankings signal a potential playoff shakeup brewing.
item.content:encoded:
The Big Ten did itself no favors last weekend, with UCLA and Indiana both losing on the road. On Tuesday night, the College Football Playoff committee delivered another reminder of how precarious the conference’s postseason position has become.

If you were wondering what chaos could look like over the final few weeks of the season, the Big Ten is living it.

Only one of its teams sits inside the top 12 of the latest CFP rankings, and there is a scenario in which the conference that produced the past three national champions sends just one team to the playoffs.

A $17 MILLION BILL FOR AN AD WHO NEVER ACTUALLY STARTED? MICHIGAN'S TREV ALBERTS MESS GETS UGLIER

All the while, it's the SEC that is thriving this week, even if that means we're still having to figure out why Alabama is ranked that far ahead of Tennessee thanks to the 'pod' system.

Though it was interesting to see Texas leap Alabama in the rankings given they have not played each other this season, so head-to-head metrics were not used.

The bigger picture involves the Big 12 and ACC, which combine to hold five spots inside this week’s top 12, led by No. 2 Utah.

SEC THREATENS THE NUCLEAR OPTION AS LSU’S REBELLION PUTS CONFERENCE FUTURE AT RISK, RJ LUIS PLANS TO SUE

Would either one of them receive more bids than the Big Ten?

The latest CFP rankings seem to indicate we are heading down that path, unless pandemonium unfolds over the next five days during "rivalry week" across the sport.

After three weeks of arguing, the CFP committee finally corrected course around the Tennessee and Alabama situation.

The Vols moved to fifth in the latest rankings, while Alabama dropped to sixth, with Texas leaping them both to third.

But, what about those Longhorns? If Texas were to play for an SEC championship next week, a loss to No. 1 Georgia would not hurt their chances of making the CFP. Now, they had better beat Texas A&M this weekend, or the Longhorns could fall straight out of the postseason.

As for Tennessee, if the Vols take care of Vanderbilt this weekend on the road in Nashville, it will be hosting a playoff game in December.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S QUIET SATURDAY TURNS INTO A BIG TEN DISASTER WITH BRUTAL CFP CONSEQUENCES

The whole 'eye test' thing was obviously starting to agitate folks, but Hunter Yurachek did note that outside noise does not factor into any decisions made by the committee, which I guess is a good thing to know given the reaction on social media recently.

"I think we all know what we signed up for in the committee room, but I'll say there is very little impact from the outside noise on what we do every Monday and Tuesday."

TENNESSEE JUMPS, ALABAMA DROPS, INDIANA AND UCLA TUMBLE IN NEW COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF TOP 25 POLL

When Alabama and Auburn get together for the "Iron Bowl," just about anything can happen.

And, even with Texas A&M looking like a $40 million waste of space this season, I wouldn’t put it past them to give the Texas Longhorns a scare, for at least three quarters.

For No. 1 Georgia, head coach Kirby Smart will have his Bulldogs ready to pounce on Georgia Tech, though I have seen a few wild endings out of that one.

There is a massive conundrum facing the conference, who has won the last three national championships.

After losing to Washington this past weekend, Indiana took a massive drop to 14th in the latest rankings. That means, unless there is pure bedlam in front of the Hoosiers, or they backdoor their way into the Big Ten championship game, the defending champions will not make the playoff.

"Indiana has two top 25 wins, but the strength of their schedule impacts their profile," CFP's Hunter Yurachek said about Indiana.

That means Indiana has dropped eleven spots after a bye-week and a three-point loss to a now-ranked opponent, which I'm sure Curt Cignetti will have thoughts about this week.

It's No. 9 UCLA that is walking a very fine line heading into a showdown with No. 15 USC this weekend in Los Angeles. What do the committee think about quarterback Ty Dieffenbach potentially missing a few games due to injury?

"UCLA fell from 4 to 9 because they lost in triple-overtime to Michigan. We will take that into consideration moving forward," CFP's Hunter Yurachek said on Tuesday night.

If you're looking for a team to make a run, I think Dan Lanning might have you covered.

Overall, the Big Ten has just a few good teams this season, and not one that stands out as dominating after nearly four months of football.

It's still No. 2 Utah holding the conference steady, with one final regular season game this weekend before a trip to the conference title game.

Where things could get crazy is if Texas Tech were to play Utah in the Big 12 title game, and then beat the Utes. This could potentially lead to the conference receiving three spots in the CFP, which would be a dream scenario for Big 12 members.

As for the ACC, it comes down to No. 6 Miami and No. 9 Wake Forest.

item.title: Steelers stun the NFL by announcing they are benching Aaron Rodgers and not letting him suit up for next game
item.description: Aaron Rodgers is inactive for the Steelers' game against the Denver Broncos as coach Mike McCarthy turns to Mason Rudolph after two straight losses.
item.content:encoded:
In what is perhaps the most shocking quarterback move of the 2026 NFL season, the Pittsburgh Steelers have benched Aaron Rodgers in favor of Mason Rudolph.

The club announced the move late Tuesday night, saying Rodgers will be inactive for Friday's game between the Steelers and Denver Broncos while Rudolph takes the reins of the team's offense.

AARON RODGERS CONFIRMS HE'S RETIRING FROM NFL AFTER 2026 SEASON WITH THE PITTSBURGH STEELERS

This decision, a source said, is not injury related.

The benching was a move from coach Mike McCarthy.

And that makes it a stunner.

McCarthy made this move one day after he told reporters, "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback."

And, look, it's not that Rodgers doesn't deserve to get evaluated like all other players. His play was obviously scrutinized and that focus includes the facts Pittsburgh has lost two consecutive games, and both Rodgers and the offense have been inconsistent for several games dating back to a Nov. 1 victory over the Cleveland Browns.

But Rodgers is not exactly surrounded by great talent. His No. 1 receiver DK Metcalf this season has made more news by getting ejected from last week's game than anything he's done to help the team win.

McCarthy must explain why he believes Rudolph gives the team the best chance to win this week. His history as starter doesn't exactly suggest he's going to overcome problems Rodgers has not.

Rudolph is 9-9-1 as a starter in the NFL during his seven seasons.

Benching Aaron Rodgers sounds bizarre and the idea that's how his career might end makes it even more outrageous.

Rodgers and McCarthy have a history that dates back to their days with the Green Bay Packers two decades ago. The two won a Super Bowl together.

'WHAT THE F--K, CALL IT!': AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY CURSE AT EACH OTHER DURING HOT MIC MOMENT

When McCarthy got hired by the Steelers in the offseason, one of his first calls was to Rodgers to see if he could convince the veteran to return to the Steelers for a second season.

And Rodgers said one of the primary reasons he returned was indeed because McCarthy was hired and because of his relationship with the coach.

That was around the time Rodgers announced this would be his final NFL season. Rodgers is in his 22nd season at age 42 (he turns 43 next month).

It's not known how Rodgers reacts to this move beyond this week.

He might request his release. He might merely accept the move, although the fact the team is going to deactivate him on Friday suggests the club understands Rodgers serving as the backup and cheerleading on the sideline is not an assignment he embraces.

Benching a four-time MVP is not a move undertaken without considering the ramifications. Those ramifications include the fact it's hard to merely re-insert Rodgers in the lineup once he's been benched.

It causes a distraction in the locker room. It also weakens if not cripples Rodgers' standing as the unquestioned team leader.

So, what happens if Rudolph struggles? McCarthy has opened himself up to the possibility of a serious evaluation of his management if that occurs.

This marks the first time in his career that Rodgers has been benched for performance.

He spent his first three seasons backing up Brett Favre before taking over as starter in 2008 and leading Green Bay for 15 seasons (2008–2022), winning Super Bowl XLV (and Super Bowl MVP) following the 2010 season while capturing his NFL MVP awards in 2011, 2014, 2020, and 2021.

Rodgers suffered a two-season stint with the New York Jets (2023–2024) marked by a 2023 Achilles injury before Rodgers joined the Steelers in June 2025 under then coach Mike Tomlin.

The Steelers won the AFC North title last season with Rodgers as their quarterback.

item.title: Marco Rubio's 2028 stock surges among House Republicans as Trump insiders split on Vance
item.description: House Republicans are pushing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to launch a 2028 presidential run, calling him the GOP's unifier after midterm losses.
item.content:encoded:
As Republicans continue to pick up the pieces from their 2026 midterm losses, one Trump administration official is catching some GOP lawmakers' eyes as the party's next great hope.

"[Secretary of State Marco Rubio] is the whole package. He's intelligent, charismatic, level-headed, cool-tempered and very knowledgeable about the issues and eloquent in explaining them," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "I think there is a lot of interest from Republicans in seeing him explore a run."

Indeed, multiple House Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital said they and their colleagues are pushing Rubio to run for president in 2028. The Cabinet official himself has publicly dismissed any talk about his future political plans, but his name is on the rise among Republicans who have said the party needs to pivot from the issues that cost them votes in November.

HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN'

"Now that we lost majorities, we can't push policy, so we will have to do better at communicating," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital on election night. "I am all in for Marco. He can be a unifier."

They're notable comments coming from the Indiana Republican, who was among the founding members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus.

MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028

Rubio has long been held up as a potential 2028 contender, despite a previous unsuccessful White House bid in 2016.

He and Vice President JD Vance have been regarded as the top contenders for the GOP nomination, but it's Rubio's name that has come up in conversations among House Republicans, Fox News Digital was told.

GOP MIDTERM BLOODBATH EXPOSES CRACKS IN VANCE'S 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS

"A number of my colleagues, unsolicited by me — they come up with me, knowing that I'm on board, [from] Miami, et cetera — and said that they'd want to support him, that they would support him if he ran," Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. " And it's not just a few. There's a number, a pretty good number, that have told me that."

Gimenez said he supported Rubio even before the election. The same goes for Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., who told Fox News Digital he's been openly backing his fellow Florida Republican for two months.

"And I think the affirmation that I'm getting from talking to people is overwhelming," Haridopolos said.

"He is not only understanding what's happening today, but our place in history. And I think his inspirational story, his parents coming from Cuba and living the opportunity that is America, and inspiring people that anything is possible is the uplifting message we need."

SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM

Both Haridopolos and Malliotakis pointed to Rubio's recent speech in Greece calling for the renewal of Western civilization as an example of his presidential possibility. Those remarks, set in Athens, were widely lauded for their scenic backdrop of the Acropolis at sunset.

And Malliotakis, who is half Cuban herself, said Rubio could "reach" Hispanic voters who largely turned away from the GOP in November.

LATINO VOTERS SWING BACK TO DEMOCRATS AHEAD OF MIDTERM ELECTIONS: POLL

"The potential for him to be the first Hispanic president is huge for our party and the country," she said.

But within the administration itself, it appears no clear successor has emerged.

One source familiar with talks told Fox News Digital that Trump administration staffers were "about 50/50" when asked if they favored Vance or Rubio.

"I think it’s pretty split," one administration official said. "I don’t think the president really knows. I think if you asked him today, he’d say Rubio."

"50/50 feels right to me," a second administration official said.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly referred Fox News Digital to President Donald Trump’s previous comments on the matter.

Over the weekend, Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that Vance and Rubio are "doing fantastically" and are "both very, very popular" when asked who he would like to see run on the Republican and Democratic tickets ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for comment but did not hear back by press time.

item.title: Trump's NVIDIA power play opens Pandora's box Democrats could weaponize, analyst warns
item.description: Eric Schiffer says Trump's push to reinstate NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang opens a Pandora's box Democrats may exploit, but national security won.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration’s efforts to re-instate Jensen Huang as CEO of NVIDIA have set a new bar for shaping a private corporation, according to Eric Schiffer, chairman and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, a crisis management and brand protection firm.

"Trump came in to really give a second life to Jensen, where he would have been dead," Schiffer told Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

Schiffer said the intervention has opened a kind of Pandora’s box that Democrats may seek to exploit to benefit ideological allies in the private sector. Still, he said the national security interests underpinning Trump’s efforts to intervene on behalf of Huang fall within the responsibilities of the presidency.

JENSEN HUANG'S NVIDIA RETURN SENDS CHINA A CLEAR MESSAGE: THE AI RACE IS ON

Asked whether he believes Democrats may use the moment as a precedent to tip the scales in favor of ideological allies down the road, Schiffer said he sees that possibility in the cards.

"I think that, of course, they would have that capability. I think that that is a risk," Schiffer said.

But Schiffer said the justification would likely depend on the circumstances.

"If the Democrats had a similar situation or it's a leading organization that is so critical to both national security and the economy, then it would make sense," Schiffer said.

"However, if the Democrats — and perhaps the future president that might be a Democrat — is empowering a crony… then I think they're going to be open to significant criticism. And I think that there would be pushback on behalf of the American public," he added.

"This is very unique and different in my opinion."

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

NVIDIA's board decided to bring back CEO Jensen Huang after he resigned earlier this month following reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence identified as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover.

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News that President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance worked over the weekend to reinstate Huang after they received security briefings and became convinced that Huang did not present a national security threat in his role as CEO. In recent days, Vance worked with figures in Silicon Valley and executives at NVIDIA to urge the board to reinstate him, the source said.

Onlooking Democrats have blasted Trump's involvement, hailing it as a presidential overreach. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, noted that Trump owns NVIDIA stock. Trump holds between $13 million and $62 million in NVIDIA stock, according to reporting from the Washington Post and its review of Trump's disclosures.

"We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions," Garcia said in a statement.

U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-Calif., echoed Garcia's criticisms.

"We will not allow America’s national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," Jeffries wrote in a press release on Monday.

Despite those criticisms from Democrats , Schiffer believes the nation’s security interests prevailed through Trump’s decision, arguing that NVIDIA’s central role in U.S. competition with China made Huang’s return a matter the president could not ignore.

"[In] the office of the presidency, you know, there's the duty to ensure that the United States continues to be strong geopolitically and certainly from a national security perspective. The move to help Jensen accomplishes those," Schiffer said.

"That's part of what a good leader and a strong leader should be doing," he added.

TO BEAT CHINA ON AI, WASHINGTON MUST FIRST EARN AMERICANS' TRUST

Apart from its reasoning for the administration's intervention, Schiffer pointed out that Trump had only used soft power to encourage Huang's return — a far cry from forcing NVIDIA into its decision through any formal use of the presidency.

"This was not a situation where the government came in under some military policy and tried to take control of NVIDIA," Schiffer said. "This was the lightest form of power."

The White House and the office of the Vice President did not immediately respond to requests for comment about whether they shared concerns about Democrats using political power to intervene in the private sector in future administrations or whether the administration had created a new precedent for corporate intervention.

item.title: How skipping breakfast to save room for dinner shocks your blood sugar and metabolism
item.description: Dietitian Gabrielle Kishner warns that skipping breakfast before Thanksgiving causes blood sugar crashes, carb cravings and overeating at the holiday meal.
item.content:encoded:
Fasting all morning to save room for a big holiday feast might seem like a smart strategy, but experts say it can have unwanted health effects, and that there are better ways to prepare.

When people go hours without food, blood sugar levels drop, triggering headaches, nausea and irritability, according to Gabrielle Kishner, a registered dietitian nutritionist and founder in New York City.

"Once we get those uncomfortable symptoms of hunger, we're going to eat really fast when we get into Thanksgiving, because we're starving," Kishner told Fox News Digital. "We're also going to crave more carbs and sugar to get that blood sugar back up."

DOCTORS SETTLE DEBATE OVER DRINKING COFFEE ON AN EMPTY STOMACH AND POTENTIAL HEALTH RISKS

Previous research has found that skipping daytime meals leads to significantly higher post-meal blood glucose spikes at dinner compared with eating regular meals.

Regular breakfast omission has also been linked to disrupted circadian rhythms, impaired insulin sensitivity and a sluggish metabolism, as well as compensatory eating later in the day.

To avoid coming to the dinner table starving, Kishner recommends eating a balanced breakfast within two hours of waking up and avoiding gaps of longer than four to six hours without food.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Combining carbohydrates, protein, fiber and healthy fats like Greek yogurt with berries and chia seeds, or avocado toast topped with hard-boiled eggs, helps stabilize energy and blood sugar, so diners arrive "comfortably hungry," she said.

If the main meal takes place early in the afternoon, a balanced midmorning snack containing two nutrient groups, like vegetables and hummus, can help bridge the gap.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

How diners build that first plate also affects digestion and energy.

Kishner recommends filling half the plate with fiber-rich fruits and vegetables, eating those first to slow digestion and help stabilize fullness.

The second half of the plate should be split evenly between protein, like turkey, and carbohydrates, such as stuffing or mashed potatoes.

Once the meal begins, pacing plays a major role in preventing gastrointestinal distress, Kishner said. Eating quickly makes it harder for the stomach to break down poorly chewed food, leading to bloating and discomfort.

It takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes for the stomach to send satiety signals to the brain, meaning fast eaters often consume far more food than they need before realizing they are full, according to Cleveland Clinic.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Kishner recommends pausing midway through the meal to assess hunger levels, and waiting 10 to 20 minutes after finishing a plate before going back for seconds.

Rich, creamy and sugary dishes take longer to digest, so sampling small portions from the dessert table helps to prevent stomachaches without making favorite foods off-limits.

For those who do end up overindulging, gentle movement afterward can ease the post-meal slump. Kishner suggests taking a 10- to 15-minute walk with family or friends after the meal to aid digestion and blood sugar regulation.

Blood sugar typically peaks 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, and even brief, light-intensity walking helps blunt glucose spikes and keep insulin levels steady. Drinking water throughout the day also helps to digest food, according to Kishner.

Above all, Kishner urges diners not to compensate the next morning by restricting food or skipping breakfast again, which only restarts the cycle of blood sugar crashes and overeating.

item.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Spivey family lawyer says no evidence points to 'stand your ground' shooting victim firing first
item.description: Scott Spivey's family attorney says audio evidence undercuts claims the insurance adjuster fired first in the 2023 road rage shooting in South Carolina.
item.content:encoded:
The South Carolina attorney representing the family of an insurance adjuster killed in a 2023 road rage shooting says there is "no physical evidence" that the 33-year-old Scott Spivey shot first, as his accused killers have alleged in court.

"I think we have the eyewitness testimony of Frank McMurrough, who says that that did not happen," said Mark Tinsley, who represents Spivey's family in an ongoing wrongful death lawsuit against two men who were charged with murder last week. "We believe that we have audio forensic evidence that supports that that didn't happen, and I think that we'll present that at trial."

Spivey died in what Tinsley has described in court documents as "a hail of gunfire" on Sept. 9, 2023, after pulling over on Camp Swamp Road, nine miles from where he first encountered defendants Charles "Weldon" Boyd, 35, and Kenneth "Bradley" Williams, 37, on Highway 9.

MICHAEL RUIZ: 911 CALL REVEALS CHASE BEFORE DISPUTED 'STAND YOUR GROUND' SHOOTING, 'HE'S TRYING TO RUN'

There were no criminal charges in the case for more than three years, after the two initially claimed self-defense and said Spivey had pulled a gun on them first in what had initially been deemed a "stand your ground" shooting. A civil judge later ruled that Boyd and Williams were not eligible for "stand your ground" immunity.

In a 911 call that Boyd placed during the chase, he told the dispatcher that Spivey opened fire first.

GOT A TIP?

But Tinsley, who questioned that the case could have ever involved a "stand your ground" claim given the highway distance traveled by Boyd and Spivey's trucks, said that in addition to the witness testimony, audio evidence undercuts the idea that Spivey could have fired first.

"Had the weapon been fired, [the sounds of gunshots] would have been captured," Tinsley said. "They weren't captured because it didn't happen."

'STAND YOUR GROUND' CLAIM FALTERS IN ROAD RAGE KILLING AS MEN CHARGED WITH MURDER, EX-COPS FACE ACCUSATIONS

O'Bryan Martin, Williams' attorney, told Fox News Digital McMurrough has said he saw Spivey raising a firearm and that the autopsy indicates his arm had been raised when he was struck by at least one bullet.

"There's no evidence he didn't fire first, either," he said.

A single casing was found outside Spivey's truck, he said, with more recovered inside the cab.

"When he collapsed, the slide on his gun was locked back on an empty magazine, so he had fired every round, and the pathologist testified at the immunity hearing that the location and angle of the wound mean his arm had to be raised when he was hit," he added.

SECRET TAPES SINK SHOOTER'S DEFENSE IN SCOTT SPIVEY ROAD RAGE KILLING

item.title: America’s first Thanksgiving was made possible by daring Revolutionary snipers
item.description: George Washington delayed the Continental Army's march to Valley Forge as the American Revolutionary War's first national Thanksgiving was proclaimed.
item.content:encoded:
By late 1777, the American Revolutionary War looked grim. The British had captured Philadelphia, forcing the Continental Congress to flee to York, Pennsylvania. Gen. George Washington’s main army suffered defeats at Brandywine, Paoli and Germantown and was preparing for a hard winter at Valley Forge.

The American victory at the Battle of Saratoga marked a turning point in history and provided much-needed good news that lifted the spirits of the young United States. Revolutionary snipers, led by Col. Daniel Morgan, would be the "Corps the [British] feared the most" in the battles for Saratoga, according to Maj. Gen. Horatio Gates.

At the Battle of Freeman’s Farm on Sept. 19, they killed numerous British officers with their "widowmakers," Pennsylvania long rifles. Before and after the battle, they acted as special forces in the no-man’s-land between the two armies, eliminating British scouts who served as their enemies’ eyes and ears, effectively blinding Crown forces.

THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER

The riflemen’s expert marksmanship proved decisive in the final battle, taking out numerous British officers, including a shot, likely fired by Pvt. Timothy Murphy, that killed British Brig. Gen. Simon Fraser. They also assaulted the British right flank, broke it and stormed several key redoubts, leading to the collapse of the British lines at the Battle of Bemis Heights.

The full story of the remarkable Revolutionary snipers and the role of the Pennsylvania Long Rifle in helping win the Revolutionary War can be found in my newest bestselling book, "Revolutionary Snipers: Washington’s Frontier Commandos Whose Marksmanship Forged a New Way of War and Helped Win the Revolution," the third book in a trilogy on the elite units of the war. This groundbreaking look at the Revolutionary War recounts the untold story of the Continental Army’s first soldiers in an immersive "Band of Brothers"-style narrative that puts the reader in the boots of these expert woodsmen, longhunters and scouts — snipers who preceded today’s U.S. Army special operators.

THE PENNSYLVANIA FARM BEHIND A WHITE HOUSE THANKSGIVING TURKEY TRADITION

At Saratoga, the Americans captured an entire British field army, a first in the war, an event that led to an alliance with France. In response to American success on the battlefield, Congress, meeting in York, appointed a committee that included Sam Adams, Richard Henry Lee and Daniel Roberdeau. On Nov. 1, Congress adopted its recommendation that Dec. 18 be a national day of "solemn Thanksgiving and praise."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

All 13 states observed this first nationwide proclamation of Thanksgiving. Gen. George Washington ordered the Continental Army to delay its move to Valley Forge by one day and observe the occasion with chaplain-led services. One soldier, Joseph Plumb Martin, recalled tongue-in-cheek the "sumptuous" extra Thanksgiving rations given to the starving soldiers: half a gill of rice and a tablespoon of vinegar before the Thanksgiving service.

States and other communities had previously declared days of Thanksgiving and fasting, but 1777 marked the first National Day of Thanksgiving for the United States of America. The Second Continental Congress proclaimed it for the whole country, as its author Samuel Adams said, "That with one heart and one voice the good people may express the grateful feelings of their hearts."
