item.title: Nation’s largest grocery chain cuts thousands of jobs — sparks fury over who it’s hiring instead: 'Insanity'
item.description: Kroger faces backlash over cutting 3,000 U.S. jobs while recruiting for a new Bangalore hub, as critics accuse the grocer of offshoring American roles.
item.content:encoded:
Kroger, the largest traditional grocery chain in the nation, is facing strong blowback on social media over its plan to slash 3,000 jobs in the United States while advertising new positions overseas in India.

The controversy comes as the Cincinnati-based grocer begins executing a three-year plan it has previously announced to cut $5 billion in costs as part of a restructuring that will eliminate roughly 37% of its U.S. corporate workforce by 2029.

While Kroger maintains the reductions are aimed at lowering shelf prices through technology and leaner operations, simultaneous recruiting for a new hub in Bangalore has fueled online accusations that the company is offshoring American jobs while asking shoppers to bear high food prices.

"‘They’re doing the jobs Americans don’t want to do,’" Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump's first term, posted on X. "No. They are taking jobs from Americans because it’s cheaper for corporations to hire foreigners."

KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Wold said situations like this need to "start to be an honest conversation about penalizing businesses that take jobs and send them overseas."

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) responded on X by saying, "Hire American."

"This insanity has to stop," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson posted on X. "Reshore ALL US companies. We’re rapidly becoming India, and I didn’t serve 20 years defending that!"

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

"Kroger says these cuts are to ‘lower prices,’" workforce intelligence researcher Amanda Goodall wrote on X. "Classic. Do you think we will see lower prices at the grocery stores? I'm not holding my breath. I'm not a boycott person... but... damn. "

In a statement, a Kroger spokesperson said the notifications "are part of the corporate headcount reduction the company announced in early October to lower prices and improve the shopping experience by simplifying operations and better use of technology." Kroger declined to answer questions regarding how many U.S. roles are being shifted to its new Bangalore capability center, the projected headcount in India or which departments were most affected.

The first wave of layoff notices went out to corporate employees last week, marking the initial phase of an overhaul announced in October by CEO Greg Foran that will pare Kroger’s white-collar workforce from roughly 8,200 to 5,200. Frontline store and warehouse employees are not targeted by the cuts.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In an October internal memo announcing the 3,000-role reduction, Foran pointed to expanding artificial intelligence and workflow automation as a central driver for trimming corporate overhead.

At the same time, job boards have listed nearly 30 corporate openings for Kroger’s new Global Capability Center in Bangalore across finance, supply chain, real estate and data analytics. Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley previously told investors the overseas capability center would deliver modest savings in 2026 before generating more substantial cost reductions in 2027 and 2028.

item.title: Senate GOP takes risky bet on Dems as holiday shutdown deadline looms: 'It's a gamble'
item.description: Senate Republicans are betting on Senate Democrats to avert another government shutdown as Democrats aim to use funding to end the eight-month Iran war.
item.content:encoded:
Congress is nearing the deadline to avert a government shutdown, and Senate Republicans are taking a leap of faith as the clock ticks: trusting Senate Democrats to dodge a holiday disaster.

When the upper chamber returns on Nov. 30, there will be just shy of two weeks for both sides to reach an agreement to thwart another partisan closure. At the center of the issue is the Iran war: Democrats intend to use the government’s purse strings to bring the eight-month conflict to an end.

Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. They have, for now, pressed pause on ramming those tax dollars through the party-line budget reconciliation process, and instead are opening the door to work with Democrats.

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

There’s history here: Senate Democrats have twice now ushered in a government shutdown. And though Republicans agreed behind closed doors to move forward with their counterparts, they know it’s a leap in the dark.

"Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

"I mean, obviously, if it's party-line, when you look at the House side, you know, we got members not showing up," he continued. "So, either way, it's a gamble. It’s a toss-up whether we try to do [appropriations] or reconciliation."

There is a middle ground beginning to form, however.

Senate Democrats are aligning behind a plan that would fund several of the GOP’s and administration’s defense priorities, particularly refilling dwindling munitions stocks that have taken a hit from the war.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has been working with a small group of Senate Democrats to produce a plan, said that while they want funding prohibitions for the war, there are some exceptions, like "defense of U.S. troops if the president seeks an authorization, evacuation of U.S. personnel."

SENATE REPUBLICANS PLAN 54-DAY BLITZ TO PUSH TRUMP'S AGENDA BEFORE DEMOCRATS SEIZE POWER

Those exceptions would likely ride on a short-term continuing resolution (CR) that would keep the government open into early next year.

He acknowledged that it was a give-and-take with Republicans, given that they do want up to $350 billion in emergency supplemental funding for the war and Pentagon, and that some limited agreements on guardrails for Iran war funding could be used as a bargaining chip for broader funding through the emergency package.

"I think there's a pretty wide recognition on both sides of the aisle that some of the munitions replacement money is needed pretty soon," Kaine said. "It's not like it produces weaponry soon, but you kind of have to start it soon."

MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT

Others in the caucus, like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., are firm in their position that the war must end.

"This is an illegal, unconstitutional and horrific war," Sanders told Fox News Digital. "I want that — the American people want to see it ended as soon as possible."

And Republicans are all too familiar with the recent history of record-shattering shutdown after record-shattering shutdown.

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital that, boiled down, the issue was about "supporting our troops and investing in our military."

"I would think the Democrats would want to support that," Banks said. "I find it baffling that they're not willing to. So I hope they'll come to the table in the interest of keeping America safe and supporting our military."

Turning to the normal government funding process, or at least using a CR, instead of reconciliation could pay off for Republicans down the line, too, when Democrats take control of the Senate next year.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., balked at Democrats’ recent history of shutdowns and told Fox News Digital that "if you always assume the worst-case scenario, the worst-case scenario is always gonna happen."

He argued that Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and appropriators should be given a chance "to say, look, we know we have areas of controversy, but some of this … spending is very, very important."

"At least try that, because then you're laying the groundwork for maybe some bipartisan regular order appropriations next year if you go down this path," Tillis said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been keyed into the ongoing negotiations, and said that there was "some interest, as you know, probably on our side" in striking a deal with the Democrats.

When asked if it was a proposal President Donald Trump could support, Thune said, "I hope so."

item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Invasive Burmese pythons push farther north into Florida as hunters race to stop ecological devastation
item.description: Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years, and now, experts warn they've been spotted further north.
item.content:encoded:
Burmese pythons have been wreaking havoc on the Florida Everglades ecosystem for more than 25 years. Now, experts warn they are making their way farther north.

Hard freezes were once thought to limit Burmese pythons to South Florida, but researchers have documented the invasive snakes sheltering and sometimes breeding in burrows, which can protect them from cold temperatures.

"First of all, they're following the food," said Amy Siewe, professional python hunter and guide. "But they are also stealing gopher, tortoise burrows and armadillo burrows. And that's how they're staying warm during those colder nights in Florida that they typically wouldn't be able to survive."

For Siewe, python hunting is a full-time job. Known as the "Python Huntress," she left behind a 13-year real estate career in 2019 after discovering Florida's Burmese python problem, turning her lifelong passion for snakes and reptiles into a new purpose.

BEAR SWIPES HUNTER'S DEER BEFORE HE GETS A CHANCE TO CLIMB OUT OF HIS TREE STAND TO RETRIEVE IT

"They eat 98% of the mammals in parts of the Everglades," said Siewe. "So they're really devastating our ecosystem. So we need to do everything we can to get them out of our ecosystem to save the native wildlife. But also, you know, we don't even know what type of damage this is going to do to our ecosystem in the years to come."

Siewe's husband, Dave, and her puppy, Dixie, like to get in on the action, too. Fox News Multimedia Reporter Amy Galo joined them on a hunt through the Everglades in Collier County, getting a firsthand look at what it takes to find the invasive snakes.

"She's (Dixie's) really just telling us where they are. And when she finds one, she says her indication," said Siewe as Dixie searched through the brush. "So then I go in. Well, once she sits, Dave calls her off, and I go verify that there's a python."

Siewe searches for pythons in the Everglades several times a week, even leading guided hunts.

"We've got our snake deck here," said Siewe. "It's a platform on the truck that just gives us a little bit of height so we can see the pythons easier in the grass and in the water and things like that."

Conservative estimates place the population of Burmese pythons in the Greater Everglades region in the tens of thousands. An exact count is difficult because these snakes are masters of camouflage.

According to Siewe, they spend roughly 85% of their time lying still in often inaccessible areas.

"We are always happy catching one, like I always want to catch one more," said Siewe. "There are a lot of times we go out and you don't catch any. That's just the nature of the python."

AGGRESSIVE TURKEYS ARE HARASSING PEOPLE ACROSS THE BOSTON AREA JUST DAYS BEFORE THANKSGIVING

More than 23,000 Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida, according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. But recently, the snakes have also been spotted farther north.

"There are two different populations. One in Brevard and also up in Charlotte County," said Siewe. "But based on what we know, the scientists think that those are separate events. So that is not an extension of the colony down here (in the Everglades) that has been established for years."

Once a breeding population becomes established, eradication is extremely difficult.

"The problem with the pythons is that you don't even know that they're there until it's way beyond your control," explained Siewe. "These guys spend 85% of their time not moving. And so, when we find one python, there could be up to a thousand more that we're not seeing."

Siewe added, "They lay eggs, you know, 20 to 40 eggs a year. Sometimes the big ones can lay over 100. So it's just, it's a never-ending cycle."

That is why researchers emphasize early detection and public education to try to prevent additional releases of captive invasive snakes.

item.title: Tuberville suggests Texans 'flee the woke-show' for Alabama after blue wave midterm elections

item.content:encoded:
Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is set to become the state's next governor in January, invited Texas residents and businesses to "flee the woke-show" and move to Alabama after historic Democratic gains in the Lone Star State during the midterm elections earlier this month.

"To any red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas… Alabama is open for business," Tuberville, a Republican, wrote Monday on X.

DAN PATRICK CONCEDES TEXAS 'TURNED PURPLE' AFTER DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC BLUE WAVE

"Texas is Black. Texas is gay. Texas is trans. Texas is indigenous. Texas is lesbian. Texas is all of us," the speaker is heard saying in the clip.

TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

Gov. Greg Abbott, who was vying for a fourth term, lost in his re-election bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick lost his re-election to Democrat Vikki Goodwin and Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico, contributing to huge Democratic gains in the state and across the country.

A trio of PETA activists crashed the Rockettes' performance at Radio City Music Hall in New York City on Tuesday in protest of the Christmas show's use of live animals in the Nativity scenes.

The protesters disrupted Radio City Music Hall’s "Christmas Spectacular" because of the camels, sheep and donkeys used in the Nativity scenes. PETA said the animals were offstage during the demonstration against the "shameful" Nativity scenes that the group argues "exploited" the animals.

During the demonstration, the activists rushed on stage with signs reading "Radio City: End Animal Acts Now!" and chanting the same message.

"No more animals on stage!" one protester shouted as she ran up on stage in front of the performers, according to footage shared by PETA.

ANIMAL RIGHTS ACTIVIST ATTACKS NYC HORSE CARRIAGE DRIVER WITH SKATEBOARD DURING TIRADE, UNION SAYS

"Keep the camels and donkeys out of the performance!" another screamed.

"Take the cruelty out of Christmas!" a third yelled.

The three demonstrators were swiftly removed from the stage and hauled out by security.

PETA said it took issue with the show subjecting the live animals to flashing lights and loud noises, including fireworks and cheering crowds.

"Unlike the Rockettes, the camels, sheep, and donkeys exploited for the Christmas Spectacular didn’t sign up for bright lights, roaring crowds, and the chaos of the stage, which can be confusing and downright terrifying for them," PETA President Tracy Reiman said in a statement.

"PETA is calling on Radio City Music Hall to listen to the growing chorus demanding that it stop exploiting animals as living set pieces and let talented human performers or clever stagecraft steal the show," Reiman continued.

The animal rights group also claimed that the animals used in the performance undergo stressful transport and are confined backstage, including some reportedly kept in the basement, when they are not performing during the show’s months-long run every winter.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Radio City Music Hall said PETA "deliberately attempted to disrupt today’s performance, endangering our performers and interfering with the experience of our guests."

"We have zero tolerance for this behavior and will pursue all available legal action against anyone who engages in such conduct," the statement continued.

HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY

The disruption during Tuesday's show was PETA's latest attempt to pressure Radio City into ending the use of live animals for shows.

Nearly 40,000 PETA supporters have called on Chase, Lexus, SpotHero and Verizon to end their sponsorships for the show until it stops using live animals.

Earlier this year, PETA sent a letter to the show’s director and choreographer, offering to fund a crafted life-size camel puppet if Radio City Music Hall agrees to retire the live animals from its Nativity scene, citing Broadway’s "The Lion King" as evidence that stagecraft can captivate audiences without forcing animals to perform.

item.title: Urban Meyer reveals his pick for the Big Ten’s top team ahead of College Football Playoff
item.description: Urban Meyer says the Oregon Ducks are the Big Ten's best team despite an 8-3 season, calling the conference's College Football Playoff outlook shaky.
item.content:encoded:
College football’s rivalry week is here.

Ohio State, the 2024 College Football Playoff national champion, will host Michigan on Saturday. Elsewhere in the Big Ten, crosstown rivals UCLA and USC will meet at the historic Rose Bowl in Pasadena.

The Big Ten has produced the past three national champions, but this year’s conference appears to lack a team that clearly stands above the rest. Urban Meyer, who coached Ohio State to a national championship in 2014, offered his take on the conference’s best team.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I see Oregon as the best team in the Big Ten Conference," Meyer said on The Triple Option podcast. "Followed by Indiana, because of defense and because of culture there. And then, I got a dotted line. Iowa and UCLA below them."

The latest CFP rankings had UCLA as the lone Big Ten team in the top 10 at No. 9. The Bruins had been ranked in the top five before suffering their first loss Saturday. Their playoff hopes took another hit when quarterback Ty Dieffenbach was injured in the overtime loss to Michigan. Nico Iamaleava, UCLA’s opening-day starter, was injured Oct. 11 and later ruled out for the season.

TENNESSEE JUMPS, ALABAMA DROPS, INDIANA AND UCLA TUMBLE IN NEW COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF TOP 25 POLL

Indiana, the defending national champions, fell to 9-2 last week after an upset loss to Washington. Despite those setbacks, Meyer does not believe the Big Ten will only send one team to the playoffs.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"There's no chance," Meyer said. "I shouldn't say there's no chance. If the Big Ten gets blown apart again like it did last week, possibly. But no, there's not."

The Big Ten’s recent run of success has raised questions about whether the SEC’s longtime reign as college football’s top conference has ended. Meyer acknowledged that the SEC is at the top of the sport, at least for now.

"The SEC is superior to the Big Ten this year. It's not close this year. It's not," Meyer continued. "Just watch the film. The speed, athleticism, you're going to see more draft picks in the SEC again, like old school. You just don't see that in the Big Ten."

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S QUIET SATURDAY TURNS INTO A BIG TEN DISASTER WITH BRUTAL CFP CONSEQUENCES

But, Meyer still believes Oregon is the one Big Ten team capable of matching the SEC’s talent.

"You do see that from Oregon. When you push play on Oregon, you see the speed, athleticism, and size that you see in the SEC. You do not see that in Indiana. Not on offense. On defense, you do."

Oregon still has a path to next week’s Big Ten Championship Game, but the Ducks have to defeat Washington and get some help from elsewhere.

item.title: Man arrested after bystanders stop alleged rape attempt inside popular fast-food restaurant's restroom
item.description: Matthew Lewellen, 39, is held on $200,000 bail after his alleged attack in the women's restroom at an In-N-Out Burger in Vancouver, Washington, police say.
item.content:encoded:
A 39-year-old Washington state man is being held on $200,000 bail after bystanders intervened to stop an alleged attack inside the women's restroom at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Vancouver, Washington, police and jail records show.

Matthew Lewellen was booked into the Clark County Jail on suspicion of first-degree attempted rape, second-degree assault by strangulation, unlawful imprisonment and indecent liberties, according to a news release Monday from the Vancouver Police Department and online jail records.

Officers responded around 1:50 p.m. Sunday to a disturbance report at the restaurant, police said.

OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO

Witnesses heard screaming coming from inside the women's restroom, prompting several bystanders to run inside, where they reportedly saw a man choking a woman, according to the release.

According to a probable cause affidavit obtained by People, the woman told police she had gone into the restroom to check her teeth in the mirror when Lewellen allegedly opened the door, stared at her, walked inside and grabbed her from behind in a chokehold while groping her body.

Her husband ran in after hearing her scream and pulled Lewellen off her before bystanders detained him inside the bathroom until officers arrived, police and People reported.

SUSPECT IN ALLEGED RAPE OF LSU STUDENT KILLED BY CAR FIGHTS TO KEEP MOM’S WARNING TEXTS OUT OF DECEMBER TRIAL

The woman did not suffer serious injuries, police said. Investigators determined the man had also attempted to sexually assault the woman, and police confirmed the two did not know each other.

A witness also told investigators Lewellen had been standing outside the restroom with his arms crossed "scoping it out" for about 20 minutes before the alleged attack, according to People.

In the affidavit, police wrote that Lewellen told officers "he knew it was wrong, but felt like she was the girl for him," and said "the voices in his head told him to do it," People reported.

Lewellen is scheduled to appear in Clark County Superior Court on Nov. 30, jail records show.

A representative for In-N-Out Burger did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ star Tovah Feldshuh has ‘no animosity’ toward co-star despite Israel disagreement
item.description: Tovah Feldshuh says Adam Brody asked to meet her privately after his Israel "genocide" remarks, but the "Nobody Wants This" co-stars share no animosity.
item.content:encoded:
"Nobody Wants This" star Tovah Feldshuh said in a new interview that co-star Adam Brody asked for a private meeting with her following criticism of his remarks accusing Israel of "genocide."

Speaking with Us Weekly ahead of a Paley Museum panel on Monday, Feldshuh said there is "no animosity" between her and Brody. She noted that she still considers him an "incredible friend," but that they remain in "profound disagreement" over the Middle East conflict.

"After he said his comments, he asked to see me. So, we’ve talked privately about it," Feldshuh said, adding that she hopes Brody will eventually reconsider his view "based on fact and history."

'NOBODY WANTS THIS' STAR ACCUSES ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE'

The disagreement began in September when Brody, who identifies as Jewish and plays a rabbi on the Netflix series, told GQ Magazine that he believes Israel is committing a "genocide" in Gaza. He added, "put me down as wanting a free Palestine."

Feldshuh, who plays Brody’s mother on "Nobody Wants This," pushed back against her co-star at the time, telling the New York Post that "to accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild." She added that doing so is "right out of Hitler’s playbook. You take the victim, and you make the victim the perpetrator."

RABBI WHO WORKED ON ADAM BRODY'S NETFLIX SHOW SLAMS ACTOR OVER GAZA COMMENTS

Feldshuh told Us Weekly that she does not plan on publicly speaking out against Brody, saying that they are colleagues and can disagree with one another without "being disagreeable."

"However, I’m sure everybody is very clear about how I stand and this isn’t a political statement. This is a statement based on whether or not I have a right to live," she added.

ISRAELI ACTRESS CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD STARS 'SILENCING ARTISTS' WHO SUPPORT JEWISH STATE

Feldshuh was not the only person behind the show to disagree with Brody. The series creator, Erin Foster, who converted to Judaism in 2019, previously said that she disagrees with Brody while praising the respectful dynamic among the cast.

Speaking on the "Not Skinny But Not Fat" podcast in October, Foster said, "I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing."

MICHAEL RAPAPORT TELLS CRAIG CARTON THAT HIS SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL HAS COST HIM WORK IN HOLLYWOOD

She added, "While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s okay."

Feldshuh acknowledged Foster's support in her new interview, telling Us Weekly she feels "lucky" the showrunner shares her perspective, and reiterated that she "will not cross swords with Adam."

ROB LOWE CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD DOUBLE STANDARD AFTER FESTIVALS REJECT BEN SHAPIRO-WRITTEN FILM

"He plays my son, and you know what else? He’s been an incredible friend to me. When they showed my documentary at the temple that hosted us, who came out of all the cast? Adam Brody. He sat next to me," she said.

Entertainment critic Christian Toto praised Feldshuh’s approach, telling Fox News Digital that the actress prioritized the show and its crew over personal politics.

"Kudos to Tovah for tackling this issue head on and not using the press to fight her battles. She's right, of course. We can all agree to disagree, and it shouldn't stop people from working together," Toto said.

He added that while Feldshuh has "more wisdom and insight into the matter than Brody," keeping the peace on set shows that she "put her show and the many people who work on it above any personal vendettas."

"Plus, ‘Nobody Wants This’ is a culture war weapon, in a way. The rom-com shows the Jewish community in a way that's flawed, funny and oh, so human. That's more important than her storming off the set or raging against her co-star," Toto said.
